dedupe_keys.name: wasteaware cities benchmark indicators wabi for 40 cities input and output data of the 2023 global analysis

description: This pair of workbooks scores how well 40 cities around the world manage their solid waste, using a standard set of benchmark indicators, and links the scores to national wealth and development. The producers are Costas A. Velis and Yoni Gavish of the University of Leeds, David C. Wilson and Sue M. Grimes of Imperial College London and Andrew Whiteman of the Resources and Waste Advisory Group, who developed the Wasteaware indicator method and used it in a 2023 paper showing that socio-economic development drives waste management performance. Coverage is 40 cities on six continents, from Monrovia, Dhaka and Lahore to Rotterdam, Singapore and San Francisco. The input workbook holds, for each city, the waste generation rate, collection coverage, quality of the collection service, share under controlled treatment and disposal, and quality of environmental protection, plus national variables such as income, human development, corruption perceptions and literacy; the output workbook summarises the random forest and regression results. Both are available as a free download from Zenodo under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence. Caveats: one profile per city compiled at different dates, scores rely on expert assessment, and national variables stand in for city conditions. Simulation uses: benchmarking waste service performance, setting targets for SDG 11.6.1 and parameterising city waste system models. Related records: Waste Atlas (data-waste-atlas) and the What a Waste database (data-what-a-waste-global-database) give wider city and country data.
name: Wasteaware Cities Benchmark Indicators (WABI) for 40 cities: input and output data of the 2023 global analysis
provider: Costas A. Velis and Yoni Gavish (University of Leeds), David C. Wilson and Sue M. Grimes (Imperial College London) and Andrew Whiteman (Resources and Waste Advisory Group)
schema_summary: Input workbook: indicators for 40 cities (waste generation per capita, collection coverage, quality of collection service, controlled treatment and disposal, quality of environmental protection) with city, country, ISO3 code and income category; country-level explanatory variables (GDP and GNI per capita, social progress, corruption perceptions, urban share, HDI, education, literacy, environmental performance), metadata for R codes and map data; output workbook: results of conditional random forest and non-linear regression models
